title: Earth, Moon and Sun
seo_title: Grade 4 Science: Earth, Moon and Sun Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
short_title: Earth, the Moon and the Sun
standard_text: The motions of Earth and the moon cause observable patterns: Earth's axis, rotation and orbit cause day, night and the seasons; the relative positions of the Sun, moon and Earth cause moon phases, tides and eclipses. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 4, Earth and Space Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 science worksheets (BC): day and night, seasons, phases of the Moon, eclipses and tides. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Earth spins once a day and orbits the Sun once a year.
key_sub: The Moon's phases repeat about every 29.5 days.
body_html:
How to think about it

Earth rotates on its tilted axis once every 24 hours, giving day and night. It orbits the Sun once a year; the 23.5° tilt causes the seasons. Nocturnal animals are active at night and diurnal animals in the day.

The Moon orbits Earth about every 29.5 days, so we see its sunlit half from different angles: the phases. When the Sun, Earth and Moon line up we get eclipses. The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, causing tides.

Example

Why is it day in Vancouver while it is night on the other side of Earth?

Earth spins; one side faces the Sun.

Answer: Earth's rotation

Example

During which phase can a solar eclipse happen?

The Moon is between the Sun and Earth.

Answer: new moon

Common mistakes

  • Saying seasons come from Earth's distance from the Sun.
  • Thinking Earth's shadow causes moon phases (that is a lunar eclipse).
  • Thinking the Moon gives its own light.

faq.q: Why are there two high tides a day?
faq.a: The Moon's pull makes a bulge of water on the side facing it and one on the opposite side; Earth turns through both.

faq.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
faq.a: It spins once in the same time it takes to orbit Earth.

items.q: Stars seem to move about 15° across the sky each hour because Earth spins. Kai watches a star for 5 hours. About how many degrees does it move?
Stars seem to move about 15° across the sky each hour because Earth spins. Ava watches a star for 4 hours. About how many degrees does it move?
How long does the Earth take to spin round once?
items.e: Day and night happen because the Earth spins; the Sun only seems to move.

items.q: What causes ocean tides?
c: mainly the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's water
items.e: Two high tides a day happen in most places.

items.q: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, which is 15° every hour. How far does it turn in 9 hours?
The Earth turns 15° every hour. How long does it take to turn 165°?
Which direction does the Sun appear to rise?
items.e: Earth spins from west to east.

items.q: Which way does the Earth spin?
items.e: Day and night happen because the Earth spins; the Sun only seems to move.

items.q: The Earth turns 15° every hour. How long does it take to turn 60°?
Stars seem to move about 15° across the sky each hour because Earth spins. Benjamin watches a star for 6 hours. About how many degrees does it move?
Earth turns 360° in 24 hours. How many degrees does it turn in 6 hours?
Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky?
c: The Earth is spinning from west to east.
The Sun orbits the Earth each day.
items.e: Day and night happen because the Earth spins; the Sun only seems to move.

items.q: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours. How many degrees does it turn in 12 hours?
How long does the Moon take to go through all its phases?
items.e: The word month comes from Moon.

items.q: The Earth turns 15° every hour. How long does it take to turn 330°?
Stars seem to move about 15° across the sky each hour because Earth spins. Emma watches a star for 8 hours. About how many degrees does it move?
Why do we see the same side of the Moon all the time?
c: The Moon spins once for each orbit of Earth.
The other side is dark forever.
items.e: This is called being tidally locked.

items.q: When it is day for us, which way is our side of the Earth facing?
items.e: Day and night happen because the Earth spins; the Sun only seems to move.

items.q: The Earth turns 15° every hour. How long does it take to turn 75°?
The Earth turns 15° every hour. How long does it take to turn 270°?
It is December. Benjamin lives in the Southern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: What causes the seasons?
c: Earth getting closer to the Sun in summer
the tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
items.e: In June the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun.

items.q: At about what angle is the Earth's axis tilted?
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: Why do we have seasons?
c: The Earth gets closer to the Sun in summer.
The Earth's axis is tilted, so each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for part of the year.
The Moon blocks the Sun in winter.
The Sun gets hotter in summer.
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: It is June. Aiden lives in the Southern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: What does a sundial use to tell time?
c: the shadow made by the Sun
items.e: Shadows move as Earth rotates.

items.q: How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun?
items.e: The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5°.

items.q: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
items.e: That is why we have years.

items.q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?
c: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth.
Earth's shadow covers part of it every night.
items.e: These are the phases of the Moon.

items.q: It is June. How high is the noon Sun in the sky where Ava lives in the Southern Hemisphere, compared with the rest of the year?
c: lower than at any other time of year
exactly overhead every day of the year
higher than at any other time of year
items.e: The tilt toward the Sun makes the noon Sun higher in summer and lower in winter.

items.q: What causes day and night?
items.e: One rotation takes about 24 hours.

items.q: It is March. Maya lives in the Southern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: It is December. Compared with March, how long are the days where Maya lives in the Southern Hemisphere?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has longer days.

items.q: It is March. Nathan lives in the Northern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: How long does the Earth take to spin once on its axis?
items.e: The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5°.

items.q: What happens in a solar eclipse?
c: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and blocks the Sun.
items.e: Never look at the Sun, even during an eclipse.

items.q: Why are shadows shortest at noon?
c: The Sun is lowest in the sky.
The Sun is highest in the sky.
It is always cloudy at noon.
items.e: High Sun, short shadow.

items.q: In December, it is winter in the Northern Hemisphere, where Chloe lives. What is the main reason?
c: The Sun gives off less energy in December.
Earth is farthest from the Sun at that time.
That hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, so sunlight hits it at a lower angle and days are shorter.
items.e: Seasons come from Earth's 23.5° tilt, not its distance from the Sun.

items.q: What causes the seasons on Earth?
c: the tilt of the Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
the Earth's changing distance from the Sun
items.e: The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5°.

items.q: It is June. Compared with March, how long are the days where Jayden lives in the Southern Hemisphere?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has longer days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the new moon?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waxing crescent?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing gibbous?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the last quarter?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Tonight Ethan sees a waning crescent. About which phase will Ethan see one week later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Tonight Arjun sees a waxing crescent. Which phase comes next?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waning crescent?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Sofia sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: New: no lit side visible. Full: the whole face is lit.

items.q: Tonight Emma sees a waxing crescent. About which phase will Emma see one week later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waxing gibbous?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the last quarter?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Tonight Ava sees a waxing gibbous. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Tonight Ethan sees a waning gibbous. About which phase will Ethan see one week later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Sofia sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Chloe sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the first quarter?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the first quarter?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the full moon?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Tonight Olivia sees a new moon. Which phase comes next?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waning gibbous?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Ethan reads: “People in a narrow path on Earth see the Sun's disk completely covered for a few minutes.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Lucas photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waxing gibbous. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waxing gibbous → waning gibbous → waning crescent → waxing crescent.

items.q: What happens in a lunar eclipse?
c: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
The Sun hides behind Earth's clouds.
items.e: The Moon can look red.

items.q: Hana reads: “The Moon turns a reddish colour for over an hour, and everyone on the night side of Earth can see it.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Ethan photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with full moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: full moon → third quarter → new moon → first quarter.

items.q: Ava photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with third quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: third quarter → waning crescent → new moon → waxing crescent.

items.q: Emma photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with waxing crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon.

items.q: Is the far side of the Moon always dark?
c: No. It gets sunlight too; we just never see it from Earth.
items.e: It is fully lit at new moon.

items.q: Noah photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with full moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: full moon → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Ava reads: “Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Hana reads: “The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Why is it unsafe to look directly at a solar eclipse without eclipse glasses?
c: Sunlight can damage your eyes even when most of the Sun is covered.
items.e: Use proper eye protection.

items.q: Emma photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with first quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous.

items.q: Chloe reads: “The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Hana photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with first quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: first quarter → full moon → third quarter → new moon.

items.q: Liam photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waning crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning crescent → waxing crescent → waxing gibbous → waning gibbous.

items.q: Lucas photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with new moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: new moon → first quarter → full moon → third quarter.

items.q: Ethan reads: “Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: When the Northern Hemisphere has summer, what does the Southern Hemisphere have?
items.e: The seasons are opposite.

items.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
c: the 23.5° tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the Sun
items.e: Tilt changes the angle of sunlight.

items.q: Scorpius is high in the sky at midnight in June. Which constellation is high at midnight 6 months later?
items.e: 6 months later it is December, and the night side faces Orion.

items.q: Why do shadows change direction during a sunny day?
c: The Sun appears to move across the sky as the Earth turns.
items.e: Link to the Earth's spin.

items.q: Pegasus is high in the sky at midnight in September. Which constellation is high at midnight 6 months later?
items.e: 6 months later it is March, and the night side faces Ethan.

items.q: Why do more people see a lunar eclipse than a total solar eclipse?
c: Everyone on Earth's night side can see the shadowed Moon, but the Moon's shadow on Earth is small.
Lunar eclipses last only a second.
items.e: Earth's shadow is large.

items.q: At midnight, Orion is high in the sky. In which month is this?
items.e: In December, Earth's night side faces toward Orion.

items.q: How could you model day and night in class?
c: Move the flashlight round a still globe.
Shine a flashlight on a globe and slowly turn the globe.
items.e: The Earth turns.

items.q:
ConstellationBest month to see it in the evening
ScorpiusJuly
NoahApril
VirgoMay
GeminiFebruary
Which constellation is best seen on winter evenings?
items.e: Gemini is best seen in February, which is in winter.

items.q: In a model, Noah walks a globe around a lamp. At each stop, he faces away from the lamp. What does facing away from the lamp show?
c: the night sky seen at midnight at that time of year
items.e: Midnight is when you face directly away from the sun.

items.q: Why do astronauts on the International Space Station see about 16 sunrises a day?
c: They orbit the Earth about 16 times a day.
The Sun moves faster in space.
items.e: Fast orbit.

items.q:
ConstellationBest month to see it in the evening
SagittariusAugust
CygnusAugust
BenjaminApril
OrionJanuary
Which constellation is best seen on spring evenings?
items.e: Benjamin is best seen in April, which is in spring.

items.q: Which model best explains a solar eclipse?
c: Sun → Earth → Moon in a straight line
Sun → Moon → Earth in a straight line
Earth → Sun → Moon in a straight line
items.e: The Moon's shadow hits Earth.

items.q: Ava sketches the Big Dipper at 8 p.m. and again at 11 p.m. What will her second sketch show?
c: The Big Dipper turned around Polaris.
The Big Dipper in exactly the same place.
items.e: The pattern keeps its shape but turns around Polaris as Earth spins.

items.q:
ConstellationBest month to see it in the evening
TaurusDecember
ScorpiusJuly
VirgoMay
SagittariusAugust
Which constellation is best seen on spring evenings?
items.e: Virgo is best seen in May, which is in spring.

items.q: Liam records which constellations he sees at 9 p.m. each month for a year. What pattern will he find?
c: The constellations change with the seasons and repeat the next year.
The stars stop moving in winter.
He will see the same stars every month.
items.e: As Earth orbits, the evening sky changes month by month and repeats every year.

items.q: Pegasus is high in the sky at midnight in September. Which constellation is high at midnight 9 months later?
items.e: 9 months later it is June, and the night side faces Scorpius.

items.q: Emma's model shows Earth closest to the Sun in early January. Why is it still winter in Canada then?
c: The Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun.
items.e: Tilt matters more than distance.

items.q: Scorpius is high in the sky at midnight in June. Which constellation is high at midnight 3 months later?
items.e: 3 months later it is September, and the night side faces Pegasus.

items.q: A student says the stars move around Earth every night. Which evidence supports that Earth spins instead?
c: Polaris, above Earth's axis, barely moves while other stars circle it.
items.e: If Earth spins on an axis, stars near the axis should barely move, and that is what we see.

items.q: Why were sundials used before clocks?
c: The Sun's shadow moves in a regular way as the Earth spins.
items.e: Regular motion.

items.q: Ava models phases with a lamp (Sun), a ball (Moon) and her head (Earth). Where should the ball be to show a full moon?
c: between her head and the lamp
on the opposite side of her head from the lamp
items.e: Full moon: Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.
